episode_title: Creating a Culture of Safety That Lasts

real_qa.q: What is Tarleton's founding year and how has the company evolved through multiple generations?
real_qa.r: Tarleton was founded in 1946, right after World War II, when Dirk's grandfather and three other partners purchased an existing company that was essentially defunct. They bought the land and the name, and after some of the older partners retired, Dirk's grandfather bought them out. Dirk's father transitioned as the second generation, and now Dirk represents the third generation with a fourth generation—his daughter and nephew—already working at the company.

real_qa.q: How has Tarleton's approach to safety evolved from physical safety to a broader safe and caring environment?
real_qa.r: Tarleton's core values—safety, quality, integrity, and enthusiasm—were documented in the mid-1970s, and the company held its first safety banquet in 1964, before OSHA was even established. Initially, safety focused on physical hazards like falls and hard hats. However, in recent years, Tarleton morphed its safety core value into building a safe and caring environment to encompass mental safety, community relations, and work-life balance, reflecting broader organizational understanding of worker wellbeing.
real_qa.requete: Tarleton safety culture evolution mental health

real_qa.q: What role does team accountability play in Tarleton's safety culture according to AGC of America conferences?
real_qa.r: According to sessions Dirk attended at the AGC of America national conference in mid-March, one of the strongest takeaways centered on team effort in safety. Dirk emphasizes that Tarleton's number-one tool in the tool belt is each other, and helping teams hold themselves and individuals accountable to one another goes a long way in building a strong safety culture. This approach addresses how office leadership can communicate safety hazards that resonate with front-line workers who face day-to-day exposures.
real_qa.requete: AGC of America team accountability safety culture

real_qa.q: What is the ASSIST program and how does it address mental health in construction?
real_qa.r: Tarleton developed ASSIST in conjunction with Washington University, modifying a program originally developed in Australia called Mates. ASSIST trains multiple levels of communicators with skills to speak to someone going through a rough time, or to someone who knows someone struggling. This addresses the fact that construction is the number two industry for deaths by suicide and has significant drug addiction prevalence.
real_qa.requete: ASSIST program construction mental health suicide

real_qa.q: What specific equipment improvements has Tarleton implemented to ensure safety for women workers?
real_qa.r: Tarleton obtained a grant to provide safety harnesses that properly fit women workers. The company has also adopted new-style hard hats with chin straps that hold the head better, and suppliers are now adapting equipment for different scenarios—reducing weight, adding sun protection, and accommodating flashlights and face shields—ensuring equipment fits all body types appropriately.
real_qa.requete: Tarleton women safety harnesses equipment fit

real_qa.q: How is artificial intelligence being used to identify safety trends and incident correlations in construction?
real_qa.r: Tarleton has started using AI tools to analyze trends in safety incidents more easily. The company examines correlations across incidents—for instance, analyzing ten incidents to identify salient facts and patterns. Dirk notes that it was previously difficult to draw trends because every incident is slightly different, but new AI tools are making it easier to spot meaningful connections and improve safety responses.
real_qa.requete: AI tools construction safety incident analysis trends

guest.bio_context: Dirk Elspermann has worked for Tarleton for 34 years and has served as Executive Vice President for many of those years. He is part of the third generation of the family-owned business, with his grandfather founding Tarleton after World War II. He previously served as national president of AGC of America and worked as a carpenter's apprentice during high school and college.
